The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)=x-{y}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨-1,2⟩$ and $b=⟨1,4⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,4)-f(-1,2) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,4⟩-⟨-1,2⟩) \\ (1-{4}^{2})-(-1-{2}^{2}) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1-(-1),4-2⟩ \\ -15-(-5) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,2⟩ \\ -10 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨1,-2y⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨1,-2{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-10 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨2,2⟩ \\ -10 & =⟨1,-2{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,2⟩ \\ -10 & =2-4{c}_{2} \\ -12 & =-4{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-2}{4-2} & =\frac{x-(-1)}{1-(-1)} \\ \frac{y-2}{2} & =\frac{x+1}{2} \\ y & =x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={c}_{1}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking into account that ${c}_{2}=3,$ we obtain that ${c}_{1}=3-3=0.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(0,3).$
